paras: The lynching of Dick the Diver was the killing of a man known only by that nickname by a crowd of vigilantes at Weeksville, a Northern Pacific Railroad construction camp in Missoula County, Montana Territory, on the evening of December 5, 1882. Accused of robbery, he was shot and, by most Montana accounts, hanged by a crowd of seventy or eighty citizens acting on a mass meeting's vow to clear the town of desperadoes. Papers in Montana, the Dakotas, Nevada and Washington treated it as a sign of the lawlessness of the camp, and none gave the victim's real name or race.

Weeksville was the terminal station of the Western Division of the Northern Pacific, and the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner wrote that the 'crowd of roughs' following the construction camp had made each terminus notorious for murder and robbery. An account reprinted in the Miner described nightly gunfire and robberies, and said that deputies who made arrests were threatened and their posses denounced as 'stranglers.'

Dick the Diver was described as a camp follower along the railroad who lived by 'gambling and robbing,' and as 'a well-known character in the western part of the Territory and on the Pacific coast.' According to the Missoula papers, his voice had been recognized during the 'rolling' of a man knocked down in front of a business house, while Pacific Coast dispatches said he had stolen $400 from a man injured by a falling beam. Before the killing, business men and others had held a mass meeting and announced their determination to 'clean out the desperadoes at any hazard.'

On the evening of December 5, a crowd of 'some seventy or eighty' surrounded Dick the Diver. The Missoula account said he 'appealed piteously for mercy,' that the crowd refused to listen, and that when he resisted he was shot through the back and a few moments later hanged. The Billings Herald said he was haltered but resisted so strongly that he was placed on the ground and shot in the back, and the Bismarck Tribune said one of the crowd shot him in the back before he was hanged.

The mail advices printed on the Pacific Coast gave a different sequence: vigilantes started with Dick and 'his pal' toward a place of execution, and when Dick shouted for help they shot him dead for fear of a rescue. In that version the companion was then turned over to the officers, and no hanging is mentioned.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the crowd, or a prosecution appears in the coverage, and the name and fate of the companion are not given.

The story first reached print on the Pacific Coast, where the Seattle Post-Intelligencer ran the Portland dispatch on December 20 under the headline 'Served Him Right' and the Eureka Daily Sentinel carried a San Francisco version the next day. Montana papers followed from December 23 with the fuller account taken from the Missoula Times, which the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner headlined as a lynching 'by Citizens' and which called the killing 'a death befitting his career.' Reprinted from the Helena Independent in the Bismarck Tribune and with an editorial preface in the Eureka Daily Sentinel, the account closed with the line that 'hell is the gainer.'

The Eureka Sentinel framed the killing by recalling the vigilantes of 1863 and argued that the people of Montana were 'required to take the law into their own hands.' Shorter Montana items were brief and approving or wry: the Dillon Tribune said 'Dick, the Driver' had 'died with his boots on' at the hands of the 'Weeksville purifiers,' and the River Press called him 'a notorious desperado.' No paper described his race, and no coverage beyond the white press of the period was available.

Accounts differ on how he died: the Missoula version had him shot and hanged, the Billings Herald described only a shooting after he was haltered, and the coast dispatches said he was shot on the way to execution. The Missoula papers' account, written closer to the scene, is the fuller one, while the coast version is the only one to mention a companion.

reader.title: Lynching of Dick the Diver
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of 70 or 80 citizens acting on a mass meeting's resolve shot and hanged a man accused of robbery (A6, A9, A12, A14).

Every account says Dick the Diver was killed by vigilantes or a crowd of 70 or 80 citizens with no legal process, as punishment for alleged robberies and to 'restore order' (A2, A6, A9, A12). The victim's race is not stated in any report, so whether this was anti-Black violence cannot be shown from the coverage.

Two independent lines of reporting, the Pacific Coast mail advices (A2, A3) and the Missoula papers' account carried in Montana (A6, A9), agree that vigilantes killed Dick the Diver; they differ on details.

framing.detail: The Seattle wire item ran under 'Served Him Right'.
The Missoula account called it 'a death befitting his career' and ended that 'hell is the gainer'; the Eureka Sentinel prefaced it by praising the vigilantes of 1863.
The Dillon Tribune's one-liner called the killers the 'Weeksville purifiers', with irony about the town.
The River Press and Billings Herald ran short news notes calling him a 'notorious desperado' and 'famous villain'.
